positions.claim: The core work of applied AI is essentially identical across verticals — moving from a hedge fund to pharma changed the domain but not the engineering method.
'Are people putting agents into production?' is the wrong question; everyone ships agents, and the real question is whether they justify their cost.
Startups fail by asking a single agent to do too much; you should build many narrowly scoped agents instead.
Most organizations already hold the proprietary data they need in unstructured form, and an LLM workflow can structure it overnight.
The prompt should encode the step-by-step mental model of the human whose job the agent simulates.
The agent scaffolding — prompts, data plumbing, observability — is not a moat because it fits on one screen and any strong engineer can reproduce it.
You should not begin iterating until you have hired a domain expert, because engineers cannot tell whether vertical output is good.
LLM-as-judge does not work in finance and pharma because the model produces plausible jargon without understanding concepts like alpha.
Models cannot verify themselves in these fields because there are no answer keys, unlike math and code where RLVR works well.
13F-style quarterly disclosure measurably reduces hedge fund returns because competitors reverse-engineer the positions.
About 30% of pharma sponsors never disclose clinical trial results despite legal requirements, and in 2026 the FDA publicly reminded roughly 2,000 sponsors.
Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has this gatekept vertical data, and it cannot be cheaply acquired through annotation labor because of NDAs and expert pay.
The domain expert should participate across the whole stack — query scoping, source curation, problem decomposition, and final judgment — turning their judgment into the agent.
Rubrics-as-rewards risks creating an echo chamber where the AI grades itself into agreement.
Error analysis over observability logs is the cheapest and highest-ROI improvement method and should precede any weight-touching technique.
RLHF is the current gold standard for gaining an edge, but fine-tuning carries recurring cost because each new base model release forces you to redo it.
The expert-in-the-loop exercise itself generates a valuable proprietary dataset of what works and what doesn't.
The Stanford AI Index figure that 89% of enterprise AI agents never reach production is wrong in framing — they reach production and fail to justify their cost.
Human-in-the-loop is premature for finance and pharma; the correct model today is AI-in-the-loop, where the expert decides and AI compresses their time.
Current models are text statistics rather than world models, so they cannot do the causal reasoning these decisions require until some future AGI threshold.
Models, infrastructure, and the tooling ecosystem are commodities; domain expertise and non-public data are the only moat.
